claims.text: Mechanical wear during tribo-corrosion disrupts the alloy's protective passive oxide film.
Passive-film disruption exposes fresh substrate that is more reactive than the passivated surface.
Exposure of fresh substrate accelerates localized corrosion.
Localized corrosion undermines the alloy's microstructural integrity.
Corrosion-induced microstructural degradation reduces wear resistance and exacerbates subsequent wear.
Reciprocal enhancement of corrosion and wear creates a positive feedback loop that increases overall material loss.
The alloy in its initial state naturally forms a stable, self-healing passive oxide layer under ambient conditions.
Mechanical wear selectively removes portions of the passive film during tribo-corrosion.
Combined tribo-corrosion will produce total degradation significantly greater than the sum of wear-only and corrosion-only degradation.
Combined exposure will increase material loss relative to the separate wear-only and corrosion-only contributions.
Combined exposure will produce higher pit density and more severe wear-track features.
The degradation morphology will exhibit signs of passive-film breakdown associated with both mechanical and chemical damage.
The proposed mechanism applies to high-entropy alloys that form stable passive films.
The proposed mechanism may fail for alloys that lack a significant passivation layer.
The proposed mechanism may fail under extremely low-corrosivity conditions that prevent relevant passive-film formation or disruption.
The relative contributions of wear-induced film removal and inherent corrosion kinetics vary with environmental parameters and alloy microstructure.
A combined degradation increase of less than approximately 20% over the additive wear-only and corrosion-only result would falsify the proposed superadditive response.
Absence of a correlation between passive-film disruption and increased localized corrosion would falsify the proposed mechanism.
